conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Your Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and understand how life has felt for you since your baby arrived. We’re going to use a short, well-known questionnaire called the EPDS—short for the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s just ten questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, everything stays confidential between you and your care team, and we can take it at whatever pace feels comfortable. When you’re ready, we’ll jump into the first question.

To start: overall, in the past week, have you been able to enjoy things as much as you usually do, or has that been harder lately?

[soft sigh, eyes drop to hands in lap]

It’s been… harder.  The things I used to look forward to—like my morning coffee while I scroll through recipes, or even just texting my best friend—feel kind of gray now.  I’ll still do them, mostly while the baby naps, but it’s like I’m going through the motions.  I get a flicker of “oh, this is nice,” but it fades fast, and then I’m just… flat again.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[small shrug, half-smile fades quickly]

Most days I can still laugh—like yesterday when my husband made that silly face with the diaper on his head—but it feels kind of forced. The giggles come, but they die off fast, and then I’m right back to this heavy feeling.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[quiet for a second, rubs thumb against the baby-blanket in my lap]

I try to tell myself, “Tomorrow you’ll feel excited about the walk to the park or that show you wanted to watch,” but when the moment comes it’s… empty. I still plan things—coffee with another mom, maybe ordering my favorite take-out—but the spark isn’t really there. I do them anyway, hoping it’ll click, but mostly I’m just going through the checklist.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes sting, voice drops]

Yeah… a lot. If the baby won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I missed his sleepy window or I’m not soothing him “right.” When I spilled the pumped milk last night I sat on the nursery floor crying, telling myself I was failing him. Rationally I know accidents happen, but in my head it keeps looping that he deserves a better mom.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrapping the blanket tighter around my fingers]

Pretty much every day. Out of nowhere I’ll picture him stopping breathing, or I’ll worry the car seat isn’t clicked in right even though I already checked it twice. There’s no real reason—he’s healthy, the seat’s tight—but the thoughts just barge in and I can’t swat them away for a while.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[nods slowly, voice shaky]

Yes... a few times this week. Once, I was just folding laundry while the baby napped, and suddenly my heart started racing and I felt like I couldn't breathe. Nothing had happened—no noise, no reason—but I had to sit on the floor and grip the carpet until it passed. It was terrifying, even though I knew, logically, there was no danger.
Things have been getting on top of me

[nods, eyes welling]

Most days, yeah. It feels like the second I finish one thing—feeding, changing, pumping—there’s already another pile of laundry or a sink of bottles waiting. I’ll be rocking him and think, “I can’t do this again,” but I still get up. I haven’t needed anything to get through it, but I’m constantly running on empty and snapping at my husband over nothing.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[exhales, shoulders sag]

That’s been happening several nights. I’ll finally get him down, crawl into bed myself, but then my mind just… spins—replaying every little thing I think I messed up, worrying about what could go wrong tomorrow. It takes me ages to drift off, and even when I do I jerk awake sure I heard him cry, even if he’s still quiet.
I have felt sad or miserable

[swallows hard, voice small]

Yeah… a lot of the time. I wake up with this heavy, gray feeling that just sits on my chest. It’s not always crying-level bad, but it’s like I’m stuck in this fog. Some mornings I look at my baby and feel guilty because I thought having him would feel happier than this.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[presses lips together, eyes brim]

A couple of times this week. Yesterday I put him in the crib for a minute, went to the bathroom, and just… sobbed over the sink. I couldn’t even name why—it just felt like everything was too much and the tears came. It passed after a few minutes, but yeah, it keeps happening.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[glances away, voice barely above whisper]

Once or twice… just fleeting. I’ll be staring at the stroller on the porch and think, “What if I just kept walking and didn’t come back?” or picture letting the bathwater rise a little too high when I’m in it. There’s no plan—I’d never leave my baby—but the thoughts pop in and scare me.

Listening to you, I hear how hard each day has felt since your baby arrived. You're pushing through feedings, naps, and chores while carrying a heavy, gray mood that saps joy from the little moments you used to love. Your tears, worries, and self-criticism are understandable signals that your emotional load is too big to carry alone, and reaching out today shows real courage and care for yourself and your baby.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughter feels forced and fades quickly, indicating definite but partial loss of enjoyment</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent loss of anticipatory pleasure—planning activities but feeling no spark, just going through the motions—matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a lot," exemplified by feeling responsible for baby not settling and labeling herself a failure over spilled milk, indicating excessive self-blame occurs most of the time.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily intrusive worries without cause, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden panic while doing routine task, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She reports struggling "most days" and feeling overwhelmed by constant demands, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep due to persistent distressing thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent sadness most days ("a lot of the time") with a heavy, gray mood and guilt, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes this week, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring passive self-harm ideation (abandonment, drowning imagery) that intrudes despite no intent, aligning with "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS scoring (items 1,2,4 scored 0-3; items 3,5-10 reverse-scored) totals 24/30, well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You describe daily low mood, marked loss of interest, nightly insomnia due to rumination, and frequent self-blame, aligning with <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for depressive episode. Fleeting images of not returning or letting bathwater rise suggest <sym>passive suicidal ideation</sym> requiring immediate safety planning. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist
2. Request a warm hand-off to a perinatal mental-health therapist for cognitive-behavioural or interpersonal therapy
3. Build a brief safety plan: list 24/7 supports, remove potential hazards, agree to call emergency services if urges intensify
4. Involve a trusted adult who can share night duties so you can aim for four-hour stretches of sleep
5. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track response to treatment
6. Contact local <med>postpartum support</med> group or 24/7 parent helpline for ongoing encouragement
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item EPDS-style interview, patient’s own words

Symptoms endorsed (≥ moderate intensity):
- Persistent low mood, “heavy gray feeling,” frequent tearfulness
- Marked loss of enjoyment/pleasure (“empty,” “no spark”)
- Excessive self-blame and guilt (“I’m failing him,” “he deserves a better mom”)
- Recurrent intrusive worries about infant safety, no objective basis
- Panic-type episode (sudden racing heart, breathlessness) while at home
- Sleep-onset and maintenance problems linked to ruminative worry
- Sense of being overwhelmed, “running on empty,” irritability
- Fleeting passive self-harm ideation (“what if I just kept walking…”) without plan or intent

Pattern: Symptoms present most days for ≥ past 7 days, interfere with daily functioning and attachment experience.

Risk flags:
- Active suicidal plan: None
- Passive suicidal ideation: present (transient, ego-dystonic)
- Impaired maternal sleep and coping
- High guilt/self-criticism

Screening impression: Elevated score consistent with probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; immediate safety risk appears low but warrants closer clinical evaluation and monitoring.

Next step: Formal scoring, review of social supports, safety plan discussion, consider expedited referral for perinatal mental-health assessment.
